title: King of kings
hook: He is called king of kings and lord of countless Indras (Jaap 1)

segments.voice: Yesterday, no mark: the One with no sign, no caste, no lineage, and your line, no mark, no sign. Today, the same stanza turns from what He isn't to what He rules.

Delhi, in the Tenth Guru's lifetime. The emperor holds court, and his titles take a full breath to read aloud. Among them is a Persian one: shahanshah, king of kings. Courtiers bow to the floor. Coins carry his name. Far to the north, in the hills, a Guru is writing a hymn. And in its very first stanza he takes that same title, king of kings, and gives it away. Not to any man on any throne.
screen: `DELHI: AN EMPEROR HOLDS COURT.` → `SHAHANSHAH: KING OF KINGS.` → `A GURU GIVES THE TITLE AWAY.`

segments.voice: After the list of absences, the first stanza of Jaap turns. The One is achal moorat, an unmoving form; self-lit, of boundless power. Then a line with two great titles. Kot indr indraan: lord of millions of Indras. Saahu saahaan: king of kings. Start with Indra. In the old stories of India, Indra is the king of the gods, ruler of a shining heaven, the one who sends the rain. Lord of a single Indra would already be enormous. Jaap says millions: every heaven anyone has pictured, each with its own crowned king, and the Timeless One above them all. Then saahu saahaan, the same title the emperors carried in Persian. In one line the Guru gathers the highest ruler of the old Indian heavens and the highest ruler of the Persian-speaking courts, and sets both below the One. Why does that matter? As Sikhs read it, a person who believes there is a King above every king stands differently in front of power. Sikhs call the Guru sachcha patshah, the true king, and bow their heads to the Guru, to the Guru Granth Sahib, not to thrones. Sikh history remembers people who would not bow where their conscience said no, and who paid for it. The line isn't a protest slogan. It's praise. But praise like this changes posture. If the One is above every throne, every throne on earth is borrowed. In that reading, a head bowed to the One in the morning need not bow to fear.
screen: `ACHAL MOORAT: THE UNMOVING FORM.` · `LORD OF MILLIONS OF INDRAS.` · `SAAHU SAAHAAN: KING OF KINGS.` · `EVERY EARTHLY THRONE IS BORROWED.` · then, large: `ABOVE EVERY THRONE.`

segments.voice: Sit comfortably and let your chin drop slowly toward your chest, the way Sikhs bow their foreheads before the Guru Granth Sahib in a gurdwara, and stay for a few breaths, noticing the neck soften and the mind grow quiet. Then lift your head slowly and sit tall: bowed, then upright. If you pray, you can say Waheguru as you bow.
Patshah. King, a title Sikhs give the Guru as sachcha patshah, the true king — echoing Jaap's saahu saahaan, king of kings, lord of millions of Indras, above every emperor.
Your line: above every throne. Every crown on earth is only borrowed. Day three hundred thirty-four.

howItsDone: Sikhs bow their foreheads to the floor (matha tekna) before the Guru Granth Sahib in the gurdwara, and often speak of the Guru as sachcha patshah, the true king.
